magic-shave.summary: A chemical depilatory powder that dissolves body and facial hair at the skin surface for smooth skin in minutes, lasting until regrowth in a few days.

quick.overview:
Magic Shave is a depilatory powder for removing body and facial hair without a razor. Skin looks smooth right after the hair is wiped away, and it sits alongside Nair and Veet as a non-razor option.

The powder breaks down the keratin in hair so it can be wiped off at the skin surface. It leaves the follicle intact, so hair grows back in a few days. In the medical literature the brand appears mainly in case reports of harm.
quick.how: People mix the powder into a paste, spread it over the area, leave it for the time the label gives, then wipe or rinse it off along with the dissolved hair. It is used on legs, arms, chest and face for a smoother look that lasts until regrowth, and is repeated as hair returns.
quick.risks: Case reports describe corneal alkali burns in 40 sailors from a powder suspected to be Magic Shave (1989) and a 2000 poisoning with respiratory arrest and potassium disturbances after a barium sulfide depilatory of this brand was swallowed. Keep it away from the eyes and mouth, and anyone with sensitive or broken skin may react with burning or irritation.

angle.text: Magic Shave is a depilatory powder that removes body and facial hair quickly, leaving smooth skin visible right after. The powder dissolves hair at the surface and it is wiped away, so results last until regrowth in a few days.

laser-hair-growth-helmet-cap.summary: Wearable low-level laser caps and helmets used at home to slow hair loss and thicken hair in androgenetic alopecia.

quick.overview:
Laser caps and helmets are worn at home with the aim of slowing hair loss and getting thicker, denser hair on the scalp. People use them for androgenetic alopecia, the common pattern thinning.

Low-power red laser light is thought to act on follicle cells to stimulate them. A 2012 review found little evidence, 2015 and 2017 reviews reported tentative benefit (10 of 11 trials in the 2017 review showed improvement), and reviewers have asked for larger long-term double-blind trials.
quick.how: Users wear the cap or helmet for short sessions several times a week, often alongside other hair-loss routines, and results are judged over months. Several devices are FDA-cleared, and prices vary widely, with premium helmets costing around $2,000 according to one forum user.
quick.risks: Reported side effects are mild pain or skin irritation. Long-term effects on skin and hair are unknown, and some devices call for eye protection during use.

angle.text: Users wear laser caps and helmets at home hoping to slow hair loss and thicken hair in androgenetic alopecia. Low-level laser light is meant to stimulate follicles, and reviews have reported mixed-to-tentative benefit while asking for larger trials.

hair-fibres-toppik.summary: Cosmetic fibres that cling to existing hair to make thinning areas look fuller within minutes, lasting until washed out.

quick.overview:
Hair fibres such as Toppik make thinning hair look denser within minutes. Sprinkled over sparse areas, they cover visible scalp gaps for an instantly fuller look.

The fine fibres bind to existing hair through static electricity, thickening each strand's appearance and reducing visible scalp. It is a cover-up that lasts until the next wash and does not regrow hair. Published research includes a 2017 microscopy analysis of five brands.
quick.how: Users shake or spray the fibres onto dry hair over thin spots, pat them in, and often set them with a hold spray. The look lasts until washed out, so it is reapplied daily, and it is often used alongside hair-loss treatments.
quick.risks: A 2020 case report described anterior uveitis after a fibre from a hair-building product entered the eye of a 73-year-old man. Keep the fibres out of the eyes and avoid inhaling them.

angle.text: Users sprinkle Toppik-style fibres over thinning areas to make hair look denser within minutes. The fibres cling to existing hair and cover scalp gaps, and the fuller look lasts until washed out.

anthralin-dithranol.summary: A psoriasis ointment also discussed for patchy alopecia areata, applied to bald spots in the hope of regrowth.

quick.overview:
Anthralin (dithranol) is a topical ointment mainly used for psoriasis that is also discussed for alopecia areata, the autoimmune patchy hair loss. People apply it to bald spots hoping for hair to regrow.

It irritates the skin, which is thought to shift the local immune response around the follicles, and it is reported to build up in mitochondria and slow cell division. A 2013 review reported tentative evidence of benefit for alopecia areata. It is not a pattern-baldness treatment.
quick.how: It comes as creams, ointments or pastes in strengths from roughly 0.1% to 2%, applied to bald patches under clinician direction, often for a limited contact time before washing off. Regrowth, where it occurs, is judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Burning and irritation are reported, along with temporary brown-to-purple staining of skin and permanent staining of clothes and bathroom fixtures. In the UK it is a Pharmacy medicine, and it is used under clinician direction.

angle.text: Anthralin is a psoriasis ointment that people apply to bald spots of alopecia areata hoping for regrowth. It irritates the skin and shifts the local immune response, and a 2013 review reported tentative benefit; it is not a pattern-baldness treatment.

coppertone-sunscreen.summary: Classic U.S. sunscreen and suntan-lotion brand used to tan with less burning and limit sun-driven skin aging.

quick.overview:
Coppertone is a classic U.S. sun care brand used to tan with less burning and to limit sun damage that ages skin. Its sunscreens aim for a more even tan and younger-looking skin over time.

It began as a 1944 suntan lotion developed by pharmacist Benjamin Green, with early marketing built on 'Tan, don't burn', and is now mostly a sunscreen line owned by Beiersdorf. UV filters as a class are well studied for photoprotection; few clinical studies concern the brand itself.
quick.how: People apply it to exposed skin before beach, pool or outdoor time and reapply through the day. It is used for holiday tanning with lower burn risk and as everyday protection for the face and body.
quick.risks: Sunscreens reduce but do not remove UV exposure, and a higher SPF still allows burning with long exposure. Early marketing emphasised tanning, and a tan itself reflects UV skin damage. Individual products can irritate sensitive skin.

angle.text: Coppertone is a classic sunscreen and suntan-lotion brand used to tan with less burning and to limit sun-driven skin aging. UV filters filter out damaging light, so skin burns less and keeps a more even, younger-looking tone.

piz-buin.summary: Alpine-named European sun care brand dating to a 1946 glacier cream, used for holiday sun protection and a steadier tan.

quick.overview:
Piz Buin is a European sun care brand used for holiday and outdoor sun protection and a steadier, less burnt tan. Less sunburn and sun damage means more even, healthier-looking skin.

It traces to Franz Greiter's 1946 Gletscher Crème and is named after an Alpine mountain. Sunscreen filters as a class are well studied; for the brand itself, published use is limited to old 1980s mouse experiments.
quick.how: People apply it to exposed skin before sun exposure and reapply through the day, choosing the SPF to suit their skin type. It is used on holidays and for outdoor sport, and some pair it with after-sun care.
quick.risks: Sunscreen lowers but does not eliminate sunburn and UV damage, and it works only as long as it is applied generously and reapplied. No human studies of the brand were found.

angle.text: Piz Buin is a European sun care brand, descended from a 1946 glacier cream, used for outdoor sun protection and a steadier tan. UV filters in the cream cut burning and sun damage, which keeps skin tone more even and healthy-looking.

bain-de-soleil.summary: Discontinued tanning gel brand, known for an orange gel and low-SPF products used to build a deeper tan.

quick.overview:
Bain de Soleil was a tanning gel brand known for its orange gel and low-SPF products, used to build a deeper tan. Skin darkened with sun exposure while the tinted gel gave a bronzed look.

It dates to 1925, when Paris hairdresser Monsieur Antoine developed an orange gel tanning formula, and Lanvin later introduced it in the U.S. Bayer discontinued it in December 2019, so it is now mostly discussed as nostalgia. No clinical studies of the brand are known.
quick.how: Users spread the gel over skin before sunbathing to deepen colour gradually. It was positioned as a tanning aid rather than a high-protection sunscreen, and people who liked the look often chose it for beach holidays.
quick.risks: Low-SPF products give correspondingly lower sunburn protection, and tanning itself reflects UV skin damage. The brand is discontinued, so only old stock or other products are available.

angle.text: Bain de Soleil was a tanning gel brand, known for its orange gel and low-SPF products, used to build a deeper tan. The tinted gel and sun exposure together darkened skin; the brand was discontinued in 2019.

boots-soltan-star-rating.summary: UK and Ireland star label showing a sunscreen's UVA-to-UVB protection ratio, helping you pick stronger UVA cover against skin aging.

quick.overview:
The Boots star rating is a label that helps you pick sunscreens with stronger UVA protection relative to UVB. UVA is tied to skin aging and pigmentation, so choosing more stars aims at less photoaging and more even skin.

It runs from one to five stars, with five the highest UVA ratio, and is based on a proprietary in vitro test. Brian Diffey at Newcastle University did the original work and Boots developed the method, which many UK manufacturers adopted. Soltan is a Boots sunscreen range.
quick.how: People look for the star mark on UK and Irish sunscreen packs and choose higher-star products for daily facial and holiday use, reading it alongside the SPF number.
quick.risks: The stars describe the UVA-to-UVB ratio, not total protection, so SPF still matters. Studies note labelling differences between regions and products with identical SPF.

angle.text: Users in the UK and Ireland read the star rating to pick sunscreens with stronger UVA protection relative to UVB, since UVA is tied to skin aging and pigmentation. Higher-star products aim at less photoaging and more even skin; it is a labelling method, not a product.

tinosorb-s-bemotrizinol.summary: A photostable broad-spectrum UV filter in EU and Asian sunscreens, sought for daily protection against sun-driven skin aging.

quick.overview:
Tinosorb S is a UV filter that absorbs both UVA and UVB light and is sought out for daily sunscreens that slow sun-driven skin aging and keep tone even. It is common in European, Australian and Asian products and often discussed in skincare communities as a reason to buy non-US sunscreens.

It absorbs ultraviolet photons and releases the energy as heat, and is described as highly photostable. A 2001 study reported it helped stabilise avobenzone and another filter under light. Research mostly covers formulation, photostability and absorption rather than appearance outcomes.
quick.how: People look for bemotrizinol (bis-ethylhexyloxyphenol methoxyphenyl triazine) on ingredient lists of sunscreens and daily creams, and apply them as part of a morning routine and reapply outdoors. Many seek imports because it has not been in the US over-the-counter monograph; a 2023 absorption study was part of work toward possible inclusion.
quick.risks: Photoallergy to sunscreen filters is described as rare in a 2010 study. A 2023 study measured how much is absorbed, and UV filters in general have been detected in coastal waters. US availability was still pending in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Skincare fans seek out Tinosorb S for broad-spectrum, photostable UV protection in sunscreens and daily creams, mainly from EU and Asian products. Blocking UVA and UVB cuts the sun damage that drives photoaging and uneven tone.

tinosorb-m-bisoctrizole.summary: A hybrid organic and particulate UV filter in European and Asian sunscreens, valued for broad UVA and UVB coverage.

quick.overview:
Tinosorb M is a broad-spectrum UV filter used in European and Asian sunscreens, valued for long-term protection against sun-driven skin aging and uneven tone. Wearing it daily means less UV damage reaching the skin.

It is a benzotriazole supplied as fine particles in water-based dispersions, and is said to work both by absorbing UV and dissipating it as heat and by scattering some light. Published work focuses on contact allergy, ex vivo skin studies and formulation rather than appearance outcomes.
quick.how: People look for bisoctrizole (methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol) on sunscreen ingredient lists, mostly in products sold in the EU and other regions, and use them as everyday facial or body sunscreens. It is not in the US over-the-counter monograph.
quick.risks: Dermatology reports describe allergic contact dermatitis, attributed in several cases to decyl glucoside, a surfactant in the dispersion rather than the filter. A 2010 study found true photoallergy to sunscreens to be rare.

angle.text: Tinosorb M is a hybrid organic and particulate UV filter used in European and Asian sunscreens for broad UVA and UVB coverage. Blocking UV limits the damage behind photoaging and uneven tone; published work focuses on formulation and contact allergy.

uvinul-a-plus.summary: A photostable UVA filter in EU sunscreens, used for strong UVA protection against skin aging and dark spots.

quick.overview:
Uvinul A Plus is a photostable UVA filter found in EU sunscreens, chosen by people who want strong UVA protection against skin aging and pigmentation. Absorbing UVA means less photoaging and fewer dark spots over time.

It is also known as diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB, Parsol DHHB), absorbs UVA with a peak near 354 nm, and is used in the EU at up to 10 percent. Published material covers chemistry and a 2020 human metabolism study rather than appearance outcomes.
quick.how: People look for DHHB on ingredient lists of European sunscreens and daily facial products, usually combined with other filters, and apply it as an everyday morning step. It is not a US sunscreen active.
quick.risks: The EU safety committee flagged a manufacturing impurity (di-n-hexyl phthalate) and recommended limits. Human metabolism was studied after oral and dermal doses in 2020.

angle.text: Uvinul A Plus is a photostable UVA filter found in EU sunscreens, sought by users who want strong UVA protection against skin aging and pigmentation. Absorbing UVA means less photoaging and fewer dark spots over time.

uvinul-t-150-ethylhexyl-triazone.summary: A UVB sunscreen filter used to raise SPF in EU products, for less sunburn and sun damage.

quick.overview:
Ethylhexyl triazone (Uvinul T 150) is a UVB filter used in sunscreens, mainly outside the US, to reach higher SPF values. It is sought in products aimed at preventing burns and sun damage to the skin.

It absorbs UVB light, with a peak near 314 nm, and is described as photostable. It is permitted in the EU at up to 5 percent. Published work is mostly formulation testing, including a 2011 comparison of fifteen European sunscreens of identical label SPF, and environmental monitoring.
quick.how: People find it on ingredient lists of EU sunscreens and use those products for daily or holiday sun protection. It is not a US sunscreen active.
quick.risks: No human clinical safety trials were found in the sources reviewed. Environmental studies have detected triazine filters in sediment, dust and tested aquatic organisms.

angle.text: Ethylhexyl triazone is a UVB filter used in EU sunscreens to raise SPF, so users look for it in products aimed at preventing burns and sun damage. Less sunburn and UV damage protects skin tone and slows photoaging.

mexoryl-sx-ecamsule.summary: L'Oreal's UVA filter in sunscreens and daily moisturisers, with human photoprotection data, used to limit sun-driven skin aging.

quick.overview:
Mexoryl SX (ecamsule) is L'Oreal's UVA filter, used in sunscreens and daily moisturisers by people aiming to limit sun-driven skin aging and pigmentation. Blocking UVA means slower photoaging and a more even tone.

It absorbs UVA with a peak near 345 nm and is described as photostable. It has more human data than most newer filters: a 1998 study reported protection of human skin against repeated UVA doses, and a 2008 review summarised clinical results of Mexoryl SX sunscreens, including UVA-induced skin changes and photoaging markers.
quick.how: It appears in products such as Anthelios and La Roche-Posay sunscreens and is applied as an everyday step on the face and body. It is one of the few newer UVA filters available in the US.
quick.risks: A 2019 JAMA trial found it detectable in blood after maximal-use application, above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold for further testing; the paper does not conclude this indicates harm. Photoallergy to sunscreens is described as rare.

angle.text: Mexoryl SX is L'Oreal's UVA filter, used in sunscreens and daily moisturisers to limit sun-driven skin aging. Absorbing UVA means slower photoaging and more even tone, and it has human photoprotection and absorption data.

mexoryl-xl-drometrizole-trisiloxane.summary: L'Oreal's broad UVA and UVB filter, usually paired with Mexoryl SX in sunscreens sold outside the US.

quick.overview:
Mexoryl XL is L'Oreal's broad-spectrum UV filter, usually paired with Mexoryl SX in European and Asian sunscreens, and sought for long-term UV protection of facial skin. Less UV damage means slower photoaging and more even tone.

It is a lipophilic benzotriazole-derived filter that absorbs UVB and UVA, with peaks near 303 and 344 nm. It is approved in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan but not the US. Studies cited tested finished L'Oreal sunscreens containing it, not the filter alone.
quick.how: People find drometrizole trisiloxane on the ingredient lists of sunscreens sold outside the US and use them as daily facial or body protection, usually in combination formulas with ecamsule.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed contain no specific safety findings for this filter. It is not approved in the US.

angle.text: Mexoryl XL is L'Oreal's broad-spectrum filter, usually paired with Mexoryl SX in sunscreens sold outside the US, and is sought for long-term UV protection of facial skin. Blocking UVA and UVB slows photoaging and keeps tone even.

iscotrizinol-uvasorb-heb.summary: A very photostable triazine UVB filter common in East Asian sunscreens, used for daily facial protection.

quick.overview:
Iscotrizinol (Uvasorb HEB) is a very photostable UVB filter common in East Asian sunscreens, where users favour it for daily facial protection. Less UV damage means slower photoaging and clearer, more even skin.

It is a triazine that absorbs UVB and some short-wave UVA, with peak absorption near 310 nm, and loses little protection under prolonged light. Research under its own name is mostly analytical or environmental, and no human clinical trial of the filter alone was found.
quick.how: People spot it as diethylhexyl butamido triazone on ingredient labels of Asian-market sunscreens and use those products as a morning step. Approval status differs between countries, and a US application was reported as pending.
quick.risks: No clinical safety trials specific to iscotrizinol were found. Environmental studies of UV filters in general are ongoing, and regulatory approval varies by country.

angle.text: Iscotrizinol is a very photostable UVB filter common in East Asian sunscreens, where users favour it for daily facial protection. Cutting UV exposure slows photoaging and keeps skin clearer and more even.

parsol-1789-avobenzone.summary: The standard UVA filter in most chemical sunscreens, used to reduce sun-driven skin aging and pigmentation.

quick.overview:
Avobenzone (Parsol 1789) is the main UVA-absorbing filter in chemical sunscreens, used to reduce sun-driven skin aging and pigmentation. Blocking UVA means slower photoaging and more even tone.

It absorbs UVA light around 357 to 360 nm and dissipates the energy mostly as heat. It is permitted at up to 3 percent in US over-the-counter sunscreens and 5 percent in the EU. It breaks down in sunlight unless stabilised, so formulators pair it with filters such as octocrylene.
quick.how: People use it without choosing it directly: it appears on the ingredient list of broad-spectrum chemical sunscreens, applied daily to face and body and reapplied outdoors.
quick.risks: Two randomized clinical trials in JAMA found it and other tested ingredients entered the bloodstream after application, with unknown clinical significance. The FDA has said more safety data are needed before classing it as GRASE, and Palau has banned it over reef concerns.

angle.text: Avobenzone is the standard UVA filter in most chemical sunscreens, used to reduce sun-driven skin aging and pigmentation. It absorbs UVA light and is paired with stabilisers because it degrades in sunlight.

octocrylene.summary: A UVB filter that also stabilises avobenzone, found in many sunscreens used for daily skin protection.

quick.overview:
Octocrylene is a UVB-absorbing sunscreen ingredient that also keeps avobenzone from breaking down, so sunscreens protect for longer in the sun. It appears in many sunscreens and SPF cosmetics used for daily protection against UV skin damage.

It absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA and is itself largely photostable. It has drawn attention for absorption into the body seen in US trials, slow formation of benzophenone in stored products, and effects on corals in laboratory studies.
quick.how: It is a background ingredient found on labels of chemical sunscreens and moisturisers with SPF, used as part of a daily or beach routine and reapplied outdoors.
quick.risks: Clinical trials detected it in plasma above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold, with unknown clinical significance. Palau and the US Virgin Islands restrict it for reef-protection reasons.

angle.text: Octocrylene is a UVB filter used mainly to keep avobenzone from breaking down, so it appears in many sunscreens used for daily skin protection. A sunscreen that holds up longer in sun means less UV skin damage.

zinc-oxide-mineral-sunscreen.summary: A photostable broad-spectrum mineral sunscreen filter, often used on sensitive or acne-prone skin and for daily facial protection.

quick.overview:
Zinc oxide sunscreens give broad UVA and UVB protection using a mineral filter, and people use them for slower photoaging and even skin tone, often on sensitive or acne-prone skin and for daily facial use.

Zinc oxide is the broadest-spectrum UV filter approved by the FDA for sunscreen and is photostable. With titanium dioxide, it was one of two filters the FDA categorized as GRASE as of 2021. Nanoscale versions exist to reduce white cast, and studies of nanoparticle zinc oxide on human skin found very low penetration.
quick.how: People apply it as a lotion, cream or stick over the face and body, daily and before outdoor time, and reapply after sweating or swimming. Tinted or nano formulations are chosen to reduce the visible white film.
quick.risks: The usual complaint is white cast on the skin, especially on deeper skin tones. Laboratory work has examined zinc release under UV and combinations with organic filters.

angle.text: Zinc oxide sunscreens are used by people who want broad-spectrum, photostable protection, often for sensitive or acne-prone skin and daily facial use. It blocks UVA and UVB, slowing photoaging and keeping tone even; the white cast is its main drawback.

titanium-dioxide-sunscreen.summary: A mineral UV filter, FDA-GRASE, strong on UVB and partly UVA, usually paired with zinc oxide.

quick.overview:
Titanium dioxide sunscreens use a mineral filter that gives good protection against UVB and part of UVA, used for slower photoaging and less sun damage. It is usually paired with zinc oxide for fuller coverage.

Fine particles on the skin absorb UV light and scatter some of it. With zinc oxide it is one of the two filters the FDA classed as generally recognized as safe and effective as of 2021. It does not fully cover the UVA range, and some products add iron oxide to block visible light.
quick.how: People use it in mineral sunscreens and tinted daily creams, often ultrafine versions combined with zinc oxide, applied to the face and body before sun exposure.
quick.risks: White cast is a common cosmetic complaint. Inhaled TiO2 dust is classified Group 2B by IARC, which is why sprays draw caution. A 1990s pilot study looked at absorption through human skin.

angle.text: Titanium dioxide sunscreens are used for mineral-based protection, strongest against UVB and partly UVA, and are often paired with zinc oxide for fuller coverage. Less UV damage slows photoaging and keeps tone even.

oxybenzone-free-sunscreen.summary: A label category for sunscreens made without benzophenone-3, chosen to keep daily UV protection while avoiding an ingredient tied to allergy, hormone and reef concerns.

quick.overview:
Oxybenzone-free sunscreens leave out benzophenone-3 while still giving UV protection for daily use, slowing sun-driven skin damage and uneven tone. Shoppers choose them to avoid an ingredient linked to allergic reactions, hormone-related concerns and coral studies.

The label is a consumer category, not one ingredient. Oxybenzone is a known sensitizer absorbed through skin, and the European Chemicals Agency identified it as an endocrine disruptor in September 2025. Critics say many coral studies lacked controls or realistic conditions, and the FDA lists it as Category III while it remains legal.
quick.how: Instead of oxybenzone, these products use other filters, often zinc oxide, titanium dioxide or other organic filters. People pick them for daily facial use, for sensitive skin, or for beach trips where reef rules apply.
quick.risks: Hawaii, Palau and other places restrict oxybenzone products. A 2022 study found multiple benzophenone filters in US sunscreens, so oxybenzone-free labelling does not rule out others. Public health bodies say sun-exposure cancer risk outweighs concerns about filter toxicity.

angle.text: Shoppers pick oxybenzone-free sunscreens to keep daily UV protection while avoiding an ingredient tied to allergy, hormone and reef concerns, which are debated. Protection comes from the other filters used, which slow photoaging and sun damage.
